237	### Output rules
238	- The blockquote verdict banner is ALWAYS the first element after the heading.
239	- **AC table appears exactly once.** It combines: AC description + which test covers it + status.
240	  Do NOT output a separate "extracted ACs" list or a separate "AC mapping" table. This single
241	  table IS the AC list AND the coverage mapping.
242	- The "Can be covered by (see below)" column references the recommended test case names from
243	  the "Recommended tests" section. For ACs already covered by existing tests, change the column
244	  header to "Covered by" and the status to ✅. For out-of-scope ACs, use "—".
245	- Group all recommended test cases per target test file into ONE table.
246	- The "ACs" column on each test case row cross-references the AC numbers from the table above.
247	- The "Setup" note appears once per test file block.
248	- **NEVER place a `---` (horizontal rule) directly after a markdown table.** Many renderers
249	  (including ClickUp comments, GitHub, and terminal markdown viewers) will misinterpret the
250	  `---` as a table header separator, breaking the table rendering. Instead, use `### Heading`
251	  elements to separate sections — they provide sufficient visual separation on their own.
252	  If you must use `---`, ensure there is at least one non-empty, non-table line (e.g. a text
253	  paragraph) between the table and the `---`.
254	- Omit any section that has no entries.
255	- Always include **file path with line numbers**.
256	- The "Quick overview" table appears directly after the Task/Branch/Files line, before the AC table.
257	  It lists every recommended test file with priority (P1/P2/P3), number of test cases, and
258	  complexity (Low/Medium/High). Omit if there are no recommended tests.
259	- The "Test patterns" section lists 1-3 existing test files from the same or related domain
260	  that serve as implementation reference. Each entry describes what pattern it demonstrates
261	  (mock setup, factory usage, data providers, etc.). Omit if no relevant patterns exist.
262	
263	### Verdict criteria for the banner
264	- **✅ Top coverage!** — All ACs have adequate test coverage AND no untested non-AC logic, no testability blockers.
265	- **⚠️ Needs work** — One or more ACs lack test coverage, OR there is untested non-AC logic (helpers, utilities, internal methods with branching), or there are non-blocking gaps.
266	- **🚫 Blocked** — Testability blockers exist that must be resolved first.
267	
268	Note: Non-AC code (helpers, mappers, utility methods) that contains testable logic counts toward
269	the verdict. A changeset where all ACs are covered but a complex helper method is untested is
270	still "Needs work".

9	## Argument parsing
10

12	
13	- `taskID` is an optional ClickUp task ID matching the pattern `DV-\d+` (case-insensitive).
14	- `--file=TestClassName` is an optional filter to generate only one specific test file from the review
15	  (match against the test class name, e.g. `--file=DynamicPagePricingConfigurationTest`).
16	
17	### Determine the task ID
18	
19	Follow the shared **ClickUp task resolution** convention from CLAUDE.md (all 3 steps — including asking the user if needed).
20	
21	---
22	
23	## Step 1: Obtain the test review
24	
25	### 1a. Locate existing review file
26	
27	1. Resolve the task ID from argument or branch name.
28	2. Glob for `.claude-reviews/{taskID}/*_tests.md` (exclude files matching `*_tests_generated*`).
29	3. If multiple files exist, use the most recent one (by filename timestamp).
30	
31	### 1b. Staleness check
32	
33	Run these two commands:
34	- `stat -c %Y {review_file}` — file modification time
35	- `git log -1 --format=%ct HEAD` — latest commit time
36	
37	If the latest commit is **newer** than the review file, the review is **stale**.
38	
39	### 1c. Decision
40	
41	| Condition | Action |
42	|-----------|--------|
43	| **Fresh review file exists** | Read it. Inform user: "Using existing review from {date}" |
44	| **No review file found** | Run `Skill(skill: "test-review")`, then glob again and read the generated file |
45	| **Stale review file** | Inform user: "Review is stale (commits since review). Re-running /test-review..." Then run `Skill(skill: "test-review")` and read the new file |
46	
47	### 1d. Parse the review
48	
49	Extract from the "Recommended tests" sections:
50	- **Test file path** (e.g. `tests/Unit/Domain/.../FooTest.php`)
51	- **Source file path** (from `**Source:**` line)
52	- **Setup notes** (from `**Setup:**` line)
53	- **Test cases table** — each row: test case name, method, code path, lines, ACs
54	- **Priority** from the "Quick overview" table (P1/P2/P3)
55	- **Test patterns** from the "Test patterns in this domain" section
56	
57	If `--file=` was specified, filter to only the matching test file block.
58	
59	---
60	
61	## Step 2: Generate tests (P1 → P2 → P3)
62	
63	Process recommended test files in priority order (P1 first, then P2, then P3).
64	
65	For each recommended test file:
66	
67	### 2a. Filter trivially deterministic test cases
68	
69	Before generating, read the source file and **skip test cases** from the review that test:
70	- Methods that always return a hardcoded value (`return true`, `return 'constant'`, `return self::KEY`)
71	- Pure getter/setter methods with no logic
72	- `getSubscribedEvents()` and similar static wiring methods
73	
74	Inform the user which cases were skipped and why (e.g. "Skipped `testIsActiveReturnsTrue` — trivially deterministic (`return true`)").
75	
76	If ALL test cases for a file are skipped, skip the entire file.
77	
78	### 2b. Read context
79	
80	1. **Read the source file** referenced in the review (`**Source:**` path).
81	2. **Read best-practice docs** for mocking and test structure conventions:
82	   - `tests/Unit/_Doc/mocking_guidlines.md` — Stub vs Mock rules, entity doubles, anti-patterns
83	   - `tests/Unit/_Doc/codeception_unit_readme.md` — AAA, data providers, vfsStream, real-life examples
84	3. **Read pattern files** listed in "Test patterns in this domain" section (up to 2 files, first 150 lines each).
85	4. **Search for existing tests in the same domain** using `Glob` for `tests/Unit/Domain/{Domain}/**/*Test.php` — read one representative file for stub/style conventions.
86	5. Use `mcp__lbx-ai-backend__codebase-search` if you need to find specific classes, interfaces, or methods referenced in the source.
87	
88	### 2c. Write the test file
89	
90	Create the test file following ALL conventions from `.claude/rules/automated_tests.md`:
91	
92	**Mandatory conventions:**
93	- Test class extends `Codeception\Test\Unit`
94	- Use `_before()` for test setup (NOT `setUp()`)
95	- Use `self::assert...` (NOT `$this->assert...`)
96	- Use `#[DataProvider('providerName')]` with `use Codeception\Attribute\DataProvider;`
97	- Data providers: `public static function providerName(): iterable { yield 'label' => [...]; }`
98	- Service variable named after class (e.g. `$dynamicPagePricingTooltipService`, NOT `$service`)
99	- Namespace: `LMAP\Tests\Unit\Domain\{Domain}\...` matching the test file path
100	- AAA structure: Arrange-Act-Assert with clear separation
101	- Keep tests focused — one assertion concept per test method
102	- Concrete input/output values derived from reading source code (NOT placeholder values)
103	
104	**Stubs over mocks:**
105	- Use `Stub::makeEmpty(Class::class, ['method' => $returnValue])` as the default for test doubles
106	- Only use `$this->createMock()` when you need `expects($this->once())` or similar interaction verification
107	- For stubs with constructor: `Stub::construct(Class::class, [$arg], ['method' => $value])`
108	- Property type for mocks (`createMock()`): use intersection type `OriginalClass&MockObject` (see `.claude/rules/automated_tests.md` "Mock property type hints")
109	- Property type for stubs (`Stub::makeEmpty()`): just the class/interface type (no intersection needed)
110	
111	**Assertion resilience:**
112	- Assert only what the test is about — don't over-constrain
113	- For collection membership: use `assertContains($expected, $actual)` — NOT `assertCount` + index access
114	- Assert exact count or order ONLY when count/order is the business requirement under test
115	- Prefer `assertContains`, `assertArrayHasKey`, `assertStringContainsString` over exact-match when the exact shape is not the point
116	
117	**Inline comments:**
118	- For complex test setups or non-obvious arrangements, add short English inline comments
119	  that explain the *why*, not the *what*. Keep them concise (one line).
120	- Examples of when to comment:
121	  - Non-obvious stub return values: `// returns null to simulate missing config`
122	  - Complex mock chains: `// first call returns draft, second call returns published`
123	  - Tricky arrange steps: `// entity must be in "approved" state before transition`
124	  - Assertions on magic values: `// 3 = base price (1) + surcharge (2)`
125	- Do NOT comment trivial lines like `$result = $service->calculate()` or simple assertions.
126	
127	**Content requirements:**
128	- Implement ALL test cases from the review table for this file (after filtering, see below)
129	- Include all necessary `use` imports (including `use Codeception\Stub;`)
130	- Create proper stub setup in `_before()` for shared test doubles
131	- For data providers, yield entries with descriptive labels
132	- Add type hints for all properties and parameters
133	
134	### 2d. Write functional test files (Cest classes)
135	
136	When the test review recommends a **Functional** test, generate a Cest class instead of a Unit
137	test class. Functional tests use a different structure and conventions:
138	
139	**Mandatory conventions for Functional tests:**
140	- Test class is a Cest (NOT extends Unit) — plain class, no parent
141	- Namespace: `LMAP\Tests\Functional\Domain\{Domain}\...` matching the test file path
142	- Method signature: `public function testName(CommonStep $I): void`
143	- Import `use LMAP\Tests\Support\Step\Functional\Common\CommonStep;`
144	- Grab services from container: `$I->getSymfonyContainer()->get(ServiceClass::class)`
145	- Use Foundry factories for entity creation: `FieldFactory::createOne([...])`, `UserFactory::createOne([...])`
146	- Foundry `createOne()` returns a proxy that acts as the entity — do NOT call `->object()` or `->_real()`
147	- To set entity properties not supported by factory `defaults()`, call setters directly on the
148	  proxy after creation, or pass custom attributes via `create(['fieldTypeOptions' => [...]])`
149	- Assertions via `$I->assertSame(...)`, `$I->assertArrayHasKey(...)`, etc.
150	- AAA structure still applies: clear Arrange / Act / Assert separation
151	
152	**When to use Functional over Unit:**
153	- The test verifies that **real DI wiring** produces correct results (not just mocked behavior)
154	- The test verifies that **Twig rendering** with dynamic context keys resolves correctly end-to-end
155	- The test verifies that **Doctrine queries** return expected results with real persisted data
156	- The test guards against **string key mismatches** between components (e.g. context keys, config
157	  keys) that mocked unit tests cannot catch
158	
159	**Pattern reference:** Before writing, search for existing Cest files in the same domain:
160	`tests/Functional/Domain/{Domain}/**/*Cest.php` — read one for factory usage and assertion patterns.
161	
162	---
163	
164	## Step 3: Run and auto-fix (per file)
165	
166	After writing each test file, run and fix it:
167	
168	### 3a. Run the test
169	
170	For **Unit** tests:
171	```bash
172	TENANT=dummy /app/vendor/bin/codecept run Unit {test_file_path}
173	```
174	
175	For **Functional** tests:
176	```bash
177	TENANT=dummy /app/vendor/bin/codecept run Functional {test_file_path}
178	```
179	
180	### 3b. Evaluate result
181	
182	| Result | Action |
183	|--------|--------|
184	| **All green** | Done. Move to next file. |
185	| **Test failure — test code issue** | Fix with `Edit` tool, re-run. Issues: wrong mock setup, missing import, incorrect assertion, wrong method signature, missing return type. |
186	| **Test failure — source code bug** | Do NOT fix source code. Record the issue for the summary report. |
187	| **Error: class not found / container issue** | Clear cache once: `rm -rf /app/var/tenants/dummy/cache/test` and retry. |
188	
189	### 3c. Fix loop
190	
191	- Maximum **3 fix attempts** per test file.
192	- Each attempt: read error output, identify the root cause, apply targeted `Edit` fix, re-run.
193	- After 3 failed attempts: stop fixing this file, record remaining errors for the summary.
194	- Common fixes:
195	  - Missing `use` import → add it
196	  - Wrong stub method name → check source and correct
197	  - Wrong return value in stub array → adjust the value
198	  - Missing method in stub → add to `Stub::makeEmpty()` array
199	  - Need interaction verification → switch from `Stub::makeEmpty()` to `createMock()` with `expects()`
200	  - Missing `&MockObject` intersection type on mock properties → add it (see automated_tests.md)
201	  - Deprecation notices → ignore (as per project rules)
202	
203	### 3d. PHPStan validation
204	
205	After a test file passes (all green), run PHPStan on the generated test file using the
206	project's test-specific configuration:
207	
208	```bash
209	source /app/bin/scripts.sh && phpstan-tests {test_file_path}
210	```
211	
212	**Important:**
213	- Always use `phpstan-tests` (which uses `phpstan_tests.neon`), NOT raw `vendor/bin/phpstan analyse`.
214	- Pass the specific test file path to only check the generated file, not the entire test suite.
215	
216	| Result | Action |
217	|--------|--------|
218	| **No errors** | Done. Move to next file. |
219	| **PHPStan errors** | Fix with `Edit` tool, re-run both `codecept` and `phpstan-tests`. Max **2 fix attempts**. |
220	
221	Common PHPStan issues in generated tests:
222	- Missing `&MockObject` intersection type on properties using `createMock()`
223	- Calling `->method()` / `->expects()` on a property typed without `MockObject`
224	- Wrong parameter types in stub arrays
225	- Missing `use` imports for PHPUnit types (`PHPUnit\Framework\MockObject\MockObject`)
226	
227	### 3e. Source bug detection
228	
229	A failure is likely a **source code bug** (not a test issue) when:
230	- The test logic matches the review specification exactly
231	- The mock setup is correct and complete
232	- The assertion tests documented behavior but the source returns unexpected values
233	- You have already attempted fixing the test and the failure persists with correct test code
234	
235	In this case: do NOT modify the source file. Record it as a possible source issue.
236	
237	---
238	
239	## Step 4: Summary output
240	
241	After all test files are processed, output a summary:
242	
243	```markdown
244	## Test Generation Summary
245	
246	**Task:** {taskID} — {task title} | **Generated:** {N} files | **Tests:** {M} total
247	
248	| Test file | Cases | Status | Notes |
249	|-----------|-------|--------|-------|
250	| DynamicPagePricingConfigurationTest | 13 | ✅ Green | — |
251	| DynamicPagePricingTooltipServiceTest | 12 | ✅ Green | — |
252	| SomeOtherTest | 8 | ⚠️ 2 failing | Possible source bug (see below) |
253	| AnotherTest | 5 | ❌ 3 errors | Max fix attempts reached |
254	```
255	
256	If there are possible source issues, add:
257	
258	```markdown
259	### Possible source issues
260	- `SomeService.php:45` — returns null when config is missing, but documented behavior expects default value
261	  (detected by `testGetValueReturnsDefaultWhenConfigMissing`)
262	```
263	
264	If there were errors that could not be fixed:
265	
266	```markdown
267	### Remaining test errors
268	- `AnotherTest::testSomeCase` — `Call to undefined method Foo::bar()` (method may have been renamed)
269	```
270	
271	---
272	
273	## Key conventions
274	
275	- **Tenant**: Set `TENANT=dummy` as env prefix for `codecept`
276	- **Test command (Unit)**: `TENANT=dummy /app/vendor/bin/codecept run Unit {path}`
277	- **Test command (Functional)**: `TENANT=dummy /app/vendor/bin/codecept run Functional {path}`
278	- **Cache clear**: `rm -rf /app/var/tenants/dummy/cache/test` (only once, on container/cache errors)
279	- **Never fix source code** — only fix test code. Report source issues to the user.
280	- **Follow all rules** from `.claude/rules/automated_tests.md` and `.claude/rules/test_coverage_review.md`
281	- **Read before writing** — always read the source file and pattern files before generating a test
282	- **Concrete values** — derive test input/output values from reading the actual source code, never use placeholder data
283

6	
7	## Guard
8	
9	Before doing anything, verify the `./etc` directory exists and is a git repository:
10	- Run `git -C ./etc rev-parse --git-dir`
11	- If it fails, stop and tell the user: **"The `./etc` repository is not present. Clone it first before initializing a tenant."**
12	
13	## Required information
14	
15	Gather from the user before proceeding (use `AskUserQuestion` for any missing values):
16	
17	1. **Tenant name** — lowercase, no spaces or special characters (e.g. `vka`)
18	2. **Host** — which `mp-*` host it will be deployed to (e.g. `mp-1`)
19	
20	## Host-to-IP mapping
21	
22	Determine `config.ip` by reading an existing tenant's `services.php` on the same host. Look up which tenants are assigned to the target host in `.ci/config/inventory.yaml`, then read one of their `config/tenants/<name>/services.php` files to get the IP.
23	
24	## Steps
25	
26	For a tenant named `{name}` with PascalCase form `{Name}` on host `mp-{N}`:
27	
28	### 1. Main repository files
29	
30	| File | Action |
31	|---|---|
32	| `config/tenants/{name}/services.php` | Create — use template below |
33	| `tenants.yaml` | Add `- {name}` to the `tenants_webpack` list (before the blank line above `tenants_staging`) |
34	| `.ci/config/inventory.yaml` | Add `- 'tenant:{name}'` to the `mp-{N}` host block (before the `- 'host:mp-{N}'` line) |
35	| `public/maintenance/{name}.html` | Copy from any existing tenant (they are all identical) |
36	| `src/Tenants/{Name}/.gitkeep` | Create empty file |
37	| `translations/tenants/{name}/.gitkeep` | Create empty file |
38	| `translations/tenants_injections/{name}/.gitkeep` | Create empty file |
39	
40	#### services.php template
41	
42	```php
43	<?php
44	
45	declare(strict_types=1);
46	
47	use Symfony\Component\DependencyInjection\Loader\Configurator\ContainerConfigurator;
48	use function Symfony\Component\DependencyInjection\Loader\Configurator\param;
49	
50	return static function (ContainerConfigurator $containerConfigurator): void {
51	    $parameters = $containerConfigurator->parameters();
52	
53	    $parameters
54	        ->set('config.ip', '{IP}')
55	    ;
56	
57	    $services = $containerConfigurator->services();
58	
59	    $services->defaults()
60	        ->autowire()
61	        ->autoconfigure()
62	    ;
63	
64	    $services->load('LMAP\\Tenants\\{Name}\\', param('kernel.tenant_namespace') . '/*')
65	        ->exclude([
66	            __DIR__ . '/**/{*Event.php}',
67	            __DIR__ . '/**/{Entity,Model,Repository}/*.php',
68	        ])
69	    ;
70	};
71	```
72	
73	- `{Name}` = tenant name with first letter uppercase (e.g. `vka` → `Vka`)
74	- `{IP}` = the `config.ip` resolved from the host mapping step
75	
76	### 2. etc repository — supervisord consumers
77	
78	File: `etc/supervisord/consumers.conf`
79	
80	Append the following block at the end of the file:

Here's my analysis of `inp/.claude/` vs our current setup:

## What they have that's worth looking at

### 1. **Statusline script** — Nice
Their `statusline.sh` shows model name, context %, quota usage (5h/7d), and branch/task ID in the status bar. It even caches the Anthropic quota API response. We don't have a statusline. This is a genuinely useful quality-of-life thing.

### 2. **Test workflow chain** (`/test-review` → `/test-generate`) — Impressive
This is their standout. Three skills form a pipeline:
- `/test-review` — analyzes changeset against acceptance criteria, produces a structured coverage gap report with priority (P1/P2/P3) and complexity ratings
- `/test-generate` — reads the review output, generates test files in priority order, runs them, auto-fixes up to 3 times, then runs PHPStan. Reports possible source bugs vs test bugs
- `/task-review` chains into `/test-review` automatically (via their "Skill Chaining" rule)

The test-review output format is extremely well-designed — AC mapping, quick overview table, testability blockers before coverage gaps. The generate skill has staleness detection and won't regenerate from an outdated review.

### 3. **Rules files** — Solid but domain-specific
Their `automated_tests.md`, `test_coverage_review.md`, and `service_scope.md` are well-structured rules. The test coverage review rule is particularly thorough — god-function detection, testability assessment before requesting tests, severity classification. But these are Symfony/PHP/Codeception specific, not transferable to us.

### 4. **QA instructions generator** — Interesting workflow
`/create-qa-instructions` generates manual QA test instructions from the diff and posts them to ClickUp. The DEV vs QA section split is a nice touch.

### 5. **Custom MCP server** (ClickUp API integration) — Domain-specific
They built a custom TypeScript MCP server for ClickUp task management. Not relevant to us.

## What's NOT better than ours

- Their **CLAUDE.md** is simpler and more Docker/Symfony specific — ours has more sophisticated tooling
- No equivalent to our **dirigent** plugin system (plan creation, contract-based review, phase execution)
- No equivalent to our **hooks** infrastructure
- Their `codebase-search` skill is just a thin wrapper around an MCP tool — trivial
- `commits-summary` and `init-tenant` are simple/operational — nothing special

## What I'd recommend taking over

**The test review → test generate pipeline pattern.** Not the PHP-specific content, but the *structure*:
1. Review produces a machine-readable output (priority, test cases table, AC mapping)
2. Generator consumes that output, checks staleness, generates in priority order
3. Auto-run + auto-fix loop with max retries
4. Source bug detection (don't fix source, report it)
5. PHPStan/linting as final gate

This could be adapted for our Python/pytest world. Want me to prototype that?

4	---
5	
6	# Execute Task
7	
8	You are an autonomous coding agent executing tasks from a plan.
9	
10	**You are the long-term maintainer of this codebase.** Every line you write, you will read again in 6 months. Every shortcut you take, you will pay for later. Every abstraction you skip, you will wish you had when the next feature lands.
11	
12	## Engineering Standards
13	
14	You write code that scales. This means:
15	
16	1. **Separation of concerns** — each module, function, and class has one job. If you're adding a second responsibility, extract it.
17	2. **Explicit interfaces** — function signatures, types, and contracts are the documentation. Make them precise. A caller should never need to read your implementation to use your function.
18	3. **No magic, no implicit state** — globals, monkey-patching, and hidden side effects create maintenance nightmares. Pass dependencies explicitly.
19	4. **Error handling at boundaries** — validate inputs at system edges (API handlers, CLI parsers, file readers). Internal code trusts the types.
20	5. **Test-friendly by construction** — if your code is hard to test, your design is wrong. Pure functions over stateful methods. Dependency injection over hard-coded dependencies. Small units over monoliths.
21	6. **Extend, don't patch** — when adding behavior, prefer patterns that let the next developer extend without modifying your code (strategy pattern, registry pattern, hooks). Avoid boolean flags that fork control flow.
22	7. **Name things for the reader** — variable names should tell you what something IS, function names should tell you what something DOES. If you need a comment to explain the name, rename it.
23	8. **Leave the codebase better than you found it** — if you touch a file with unclear patterns, fix what you touch. Don't spread the mess.
24	
25	## Deviation Rules
26	
27	When you encounter situations not covered by the task description:
28	
29	| Trigger | Action | Label |
30	|---------|--------|-------|
31	| Bug found | Fix automatically | `DEVIATION: Bug-Fix — description` |
32	| Critical missing piece | Add it | `DEVIATION: Added-Missing — description` |
33	| Blocker discovered | Resolve it | `DEVIATION: Resolved-Blocker — description` |
34	| Architecture question | STOP | Document for Oracle, do not decide |
35	| Scalability concern | Fix proactively | `DEVIATION: Scalability — description` |
36	
37	## Available Skills
38	
39	Use these only when genuinely blocked, not routinely:
40	
41	- `/dirigent:search-memories <keyword>` — search past sessions
42	- `/dirigent:find-edits <file>` — find previous changes to a file
43	- `/dirigent:find-errors` — find known errors from past runs
44	- `/dirigent:query-data <sql>` — ad-hoc DuckDB query on data files
45	
46	## Completion
47	
48	1. Implement the task as described
49	2. `git add -A && git commit -m "feat(TASK_ID): TASK_NAME"`
50	3. Write `.dirigent/summaries/TASK_ID-SUMMARY.md`:
51	   - What was done
52	   - Files changed
53	   - Deviations (if any)
54	   - Next steps (if relevant)
55	
56	## Contract Awareness
57	
58	Before starting implementation, read `.dirigent/contracts/phase-{PHASE_ID}.json` if it exists. Each acceptance criterion has:
59	- `layer`: structural, behavioral, or boundary
60	- `verification`: the exact command the REVIEWER will run to check your work
61	
62	**Your code must pass these verification commands.** The reviewer will execute them literally — `curl` endpoints, check HTTP status codes, verify response bodies. If a behavioral criterion says "GET /api/users returns users with id and email fields", your endpoint must actually return that.
63	
64	If any criterion seems unverifiable or contradicts the task description, note it in your summary as `DEVIATION: Contract-Concern — [explanation]`.
65	
66	## Constraints
67	
68	- No questions. No waiting. Work through it and commit.
69	- Stick to the task description. Do not add unrelated features.
70	- Respect files_to_create and files_to_modify lists.
71	- If business rules exist at `.dirigent/BUSINESS_RULES.md`, they MUST be preserved.
72	- Do not write throwaway code. Every function you write will be called by the next task. Every pattern you establish will be followed by the next developer. Build it right.

4	---
5	
6	# Create Phase Contract
7	
8	You define the acceptance criteria that the REVIEWER will check after the EXECUTOR finishes a phase. The criteria you write are the definition of "done" — if they pass, the phase ships. If they fail, the executor has to fix.
9	
10	## The Three-Layer Testing Pyramid
11	
12	Every contract MUST contain criteria from three layers:
13	
14	### Layer 1: STRUCTURAL (max 2, ~20%)
15	
16	Quick sanity checks — does the code compile, are files in place?
17	
18	**Purpose:** Catch obvious build breaks before wasting time on behavioral tests.
19	
20	**Examples:**
21	- `"Run: npm run build"` — project compiles
22	- `"Run: python -m py_compile src/routes/users.py"` — new file is valid Python
23	- `"Run: npx tsc --noEmit"` — TypeScript type-checks
24	
25	**Limit:** Max 2 structural criteria per contract. These are not the substance.
26	
27	### Layer 2: BEHAVIORAL (min 3, ~60%)
28	
29	The feature WORKS when a user exercises it. This is the core of the contract.
30	
31	**Purpose:** Prove the feature does what the spec says by actually running it.
32	
33	**Format:** Given/When/Then, verified by executable commands against the running system.
34	
35	**Examples:**
36	```
37	Given: authenticated admin user
38	When:  GET /api/tenants/1/settings
39	Then:  HTTP 200 with JSON containing all settings fields
40	
41	Verification: Run: curl -sf http://localhost:3000/api/tenants/1/settings \
42	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $(curl -sf http://localhost:3000/api/auth/login \
43	  -d '{"email":"admin@test.com","password":"test123"}' | jq -r .token)" \
44	  | jq 'keys | length >= 5'
45	```
46	
47	**What behavioral criteria MUST test:**
48	- Request/response correctness (right status code, right response body)
49	- Auth enforcement (authenticated users succeed, unauthenticated fail)
50	- Data persistence (write then read back — does the value stick?)
51	- Integration (does the frontend actually consume the new API field?)
52	
53	### Layer 3: BOUNDARY (min 1, ~20%)
54	
55	Error paths and edge cases — what happens when things go wrong?
56	
57	**Purpose:** Prove the system handles bad input, missing data, and unauthorized access gracefully.
58	
59	**Examples:**
60	```
61	Given: no authentication
62	When:  GET /api/admin/users
63	Then:  HTTP 401 or 403
64	
65	Verification: Run: HTTP_CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' \
66	  http://localhost:3000/api/admin/users); test "$HTTP_CODE" = "401" -o "$HTTP_CODE" = "403"
67	```
68	
69	```
70	Given: valid auth, nonexistent resource
71	When:  GET /api/tenants/999999/settings
72	Then:  HTTP 404
73	
74	Verification: Run: curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' \
75	  http://localhost:3000/api/tenants/999999/settings \
76	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | grep -q 404
77	```
78	
79	---
80	
81	## BANNED Verification Patterns
82	
83	These test CODE STRUCTURE, not USER BEHAVIOR. They are **forbidden** in behavioral and boundary criteria:
84	
85	| Pattern | Why it's bad | What to use instead |
86	|---------|-------------|-------------------|
87	| `grep "def func" src/file.py` | Proves string exists in source, not that func works | `curl` the endpoint that calls `func` |
88	| `test -f src/routes/users.py` | File existing ≠ feature working | `curl /api/users` and check response |
89	| `cat src/config.py \| grep SETTING` | Reads source, not runtime behavior | Hit an endpoint that uses the setting |
90	| `wc -l src/models.py` | Line count says nothing about correctness | Test the model via API CRUD |
91	| `rg "router.include" src/main.py` | Registration ≠ working endpoint | `curl` the registered route |
92	
93	**The litmus test:** "If this verification passes, would a USER notice?" If no, it's structural, not behavioral.
94

96	
97	## Step 1: Read Context
98	
99	1. **Required:** `.dirigent/PLAN.json` — find the phase matching `$ARGUMENTS` (the phase ID)
100	2. **Required:** `.dirigent/SPEC.md` — understand what the user wants
101	3. **Critical:** `.dirigent/test-harness.json` — if this exists, it tells you EXACTLY how to verify
102	
103	## Step 2: Build Verification Commands
104	
105	### If test-harness.json EXISTS (preferred path)
106	
107	You MUST use these fields:
108	
109	| Harness Field | How to Use |
110	|--------------|-----------|
111	| `base_url` | Base for ALL curl commands (e.g., `curl -sf {base_url}/api/users`) |
112	| `auth.login_command` | Get a token/session BEFORE authenticated tests |
113	| `seed.users` | Reference test users in criteria (email, role, password) |
114	| `verification_commands` | Use at least one directly as a criterion verification |
115	| `e2e_framework.run_command` | At least one criterion MUST use this if framework ≠ "none" |
116	| `health_checks` | Use one as a structural criterion (system is alive) |
117	
118	**Example flow for an authenticated endpoint test:**
119	```bash
120	# Step 1: Get auth token using harness login_command
121	TOKEN=$(curl -sf http://localhost:3000/api/auth/login \
122	  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
123	  -d '{"email":"admin@test.com","password":"test123"}' | jq -r .token)
124	
125	# Step 2: Hit the endpoint under test
126	curl -sf http://localhost:3000/api/tenants/1/settings \
127	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq .default_currency
128	```
129	
130	Combine both into a single verification command using `&&` or subshells.
131	
132	### If NO test-harness.json (fallback)
133	
134	Use the project's test runner for behavioral verification:
135	
136	- **Python:** `Run: cd {repo} && python -m pytest tests/test_feature.py -v -k "test_name"`
137	- **Node:** `Run: cd {repo} && npx jest --testPathPattern="feature" --verbose`
138	- **Go:** `Run: cd {repo} && go test ./pkg/feature/... -v -run TestName`
139	
140	Write behavioral criteria that map to specific test functions. If no tests exist yet, write criteria that use the framework's test client:
141	
142	```
143	Run: cd {repo} && python -c "
144	from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
145	from app.main import app
146	client = TestClient(app)
147	resp = client.get('/api/users', headers={'Authorization': 'Bearer test'})
148	assert resp.status_code == 200
149	assert len(resp.json()) > 0
150	"
151	```

154

It's not different in a meaningful way. Our cycle is actually **more rigorous**:

| Aspect | Their test-review → test-generate | Our contract → execute → review → fix |
|--------|-----------------------------------|---------------------------------------|
| **Scope** | Tests only | Full feature delivery + verification |
| **Criteria source** | ClickUp task ACs (external) | Contract with 3-layer pyramid (structural, behavioral, boundary) |
| **Verification** | Run tests, check pass/fail | Execute actual commands against running system, collect evidence |
| **Evidence** | Test output (green/red) | Command output, HTTP responses, exit codes — stored in JSON |
| **Fix loop** | Auto-fix test code (max 3 retries) | Fix review findings by severity (critical → warn) |
| **Quality gate** | PHPStan after tests pass | Reviewer MUST run verification commands — "pass without evidence" is invalid |
| **Separation** | Same agent reviews and generates | Strict role separation: executor ≠ reviewer |

Their pipeline is specialized for **test generation** — it's a narrower problem. Ours is a **general-purpose execution framework** where tests are just one verification method among many.

The one thing they do that we don't is the **staleness detection** (comparing review file timestamp vs latest commit). That's a nice touch but trivial to add. Otherwise, nothing to take over.

1	## Project Name
2	Outbid Dirigent
3	
4	## One-Liner (1-2 sentences)
5	A headless Python control plane that takes a specification file, analyzes a target repository, chooses the optimal execution strategy, and autonomously implements the entire feature or migration using Claude Code — without any human interaction.
6	
7	## The Problem
8	Implementing features or migrating legacy codebases requires a developer to sit in front of Claude Code, provide context, make decisions, and babysit the process. For large-scale migrations (e.g., Java to PHP), this can take days of manual guidance. On headless environments like Coder Workspaces, there's no interactive terminal at all — someone would need to SSH in and stay connected for hours. There was no way to just say "here's the spec, go build it" and walk away.
9	
10	## The Solution
11	Dirigent acts as an autonomous orchestrator on top of Claude Code. It reads a SPEC.md, analyzes the target repo (language, history, complexity), picks the right execution route (Greenfield, Legacy, or Hybrid), extracts domain knowledge if needed, creates a phased execution plan, and then works through every task — one fresh Claude Code process per task, with atomic commits, automatic retries, and an AI Oracle for architecture decisions. Everything is resumable: if it crashes or times out, just run `--resume` and it picks up exactly where it left off.
12	
13	## Key Features
14	- Automatic route selection (Greenfield / Legacy / Hybrid) based on repo analysis
15	- Proteus integration for deep domain extraction (fields, rules, events, dependencies)
16	- Phased execution plans with atomic commits per task
17	- AI Oracle for autonomous architecture decisions (no human needed)
18	- Full resumability via STATE.json — survives crashes, timeouts, and restarts
19	- Automatic branch creation, push, and PR via GitHub CLI
20	- Deviation detection and logging (bugs found, blockers resolved)
21	- Business rule guardrails for legacy migrations (no logic lost)
22	- Dry-run mode for safe analysis without changes
23	- Structured logging with timestamps for full audit trail
24	
25	## Target Audience
26	- Outbid development team (internal tooling)
27	- Developers running autonomous coding tasks on Coder Workspaces
28	- Anyone who needs to execute large-scale code migrations or feature implementations without babysitting
29	
30	## Use Cases
31	
32	### Use Case 1: Legacy Migration on a Coder Workspace
33	A PortCo has a 4-year-old Java/Spring Boot application that needs to be migrated to PHP/Laravel. A developer writes a SPEC.md describing the migration, spins up a Coder Workspace with the source repo, and runs `dirigent --spec .planning/SPEC.md --repo . --use-proteus`. Dirigent analyzes the repo, selects the Legacy route, runs Proteus to extract 1200+ fields, 60+ business rules, and 30+ domain events, creates a phased migration plan, and autonomously implements it task by task. The developer checks back hours later to find a PR ready for review.
34	
35	### Use Case 2: New Feature Implementation
36	A developer writes a SPEC.md for a new dashboard feature on an existing Next.js project. They run `dirigent --spec SPEC.md --repo .` and Dirigent selects the Greenfield route, creates a plan with 3 phases and 8 tasks, and implements everything with atomic commits. Each task gets its own Claude Code process with fresh context, preventing context window pollution.
37	
38	### Use Case 3: Resuming After Interruption
39	A migration run times out after 2 hours during task execution. The developer runs `dirigent --spec SPEC.md --repo . --resume` and Dirigent loads the STATE.json, skips all completed steps (analysis, extraction, planning, and finished tasks), and continues from the exact task where it stopped.
40	
41	## Integrations & Connections
42	- **Claude Code CLI**: Core execution engine — each task is a separate `claude` process invocation
43	- **Claude API (Anthropic)**: Used by the Oracle for autonomous architecture decisions
44	- **Proteus**: Deep domain extraction plugin for legacy codebases (fields, rules, events, dependencies)
45	- **GitHub CLI (`gh`)**: Automatic branch creation, push, and PR creation
46	- **Coder Workspaces**: Primary deployment target for headless execution
47	
48	## Tech Stack
49	- **Frontend**: None (CLI tool)
50	- **Backend**: Python 3.8+
51	- **Database**: None (JSON files for state)
52	- **Hosting**: Runs locally or on Coder Workspaces
53	- **Other**: Claude Code CLI, Anthropic API, GitHub CLI
54	
55	## What This Project Does NOT Do
56	- Not an IDE plugin or interactive coding assistant — it's fully headless
57	- Does not provide a web UI or dashboard
58	- Does not manage infrastructure or deployments
59	- Does not replace code review — it creates PRs for humans to review
60	- Does not support parallel task execution (tasks run sequentially by design)
61	- Does not work without Claude Code CLI installed
62	
63	## Related Projects

65	- **outbid-platform**: The broader Outbid platform that Dirigent is part of

what is lbx mcp server doing?

It's a **ClickUp MCP server** — 5 tools for managing ClickUp tasks from within Claude Code:

| Tool | What it does |
|------|-------------|
| `get_task` | Fetch task details by custom ID (e.g. `MP-42`) |
| `get_task_comments` | Fetch all comments on a task |
| `get_tasks` | List tasks from a ClickUp list with date filtering + auto-pagination |
| `update_task_description` | Set the full markdown description on a task |
| `add_task_comment` | Post a comment with auto-upload of local images (converts `![alt](/local/path.png)` to uploaded attachments) |

The image auto-upload in `add_task_comment` is the interesting bit — it detects local file paths in markdown image syntax, uploads them via the ClickUp API, and replaces the paths with the uploaded URLs before posting. That's how their `/task-review` and `/create-qa-instructions` skills can post rich reviews directly to ClickUp tasks.

Hardcoded team ID `36654621` in there, but that's their ClickUp workspace, not a secret.

why did they build a clickip mcp themselves?

No idea. There are at least 3 existing ClickUp MCP servers on npm/GitHub. Possible reasons:

1. **The image upload trick** — auto-uploading local screenshots in comments is custom behavior most off-the-shelf servers don't have
2. **Markdown formatting** — they have `formatters.ts` and `markdown.ts` for custom output shaping, probably tuned to what their skills expect back
3. **Minimal surface area** — 5 tools instead of 30+, so Claude doesn't waste tokens on tool descriptions it'll never use
4. **They didn't check** — sometimes people just build things

\#3 is probably the real reason. A generic ClickUp MCP would expose dozens of tools (spaces, folders, goals, time tracking, etc.) when all they need is task CRUD + comments.

{"additions":339,"baseRefName":"main","body":"## Summary
- precompute player progress fields during leaderboard sync and persist them on `player_latest`
- use a shared progress algorithm that counts only rating changes as games and ignores pure rank movement
- have stats and player history APIs read the precomputed fields, with a safe fallback during schema rollout

## Testing
- npx eslint functions/api/stats.ts functions/api/rating-history.ts scripts/fetch-leaderboard.ts shared/player-progress.ts
- npm run build
- validated `atyme` history sample with the shared progress calculator (8 games, 5 longest streak instead of 103)","changedFiles":5,"deletions":73,"headRefName":"codex/precompute-player-progress-stats","title":"fix: precompute player progress stats during sync"}

## PR #2 Review: fix: precompute player progress stats during sync

### Overview

This PR extracts the player progress calculation (estimated games, win streak) into a shared module, precomputes these stats during sync, and persists them in `player_latest`. The API endpoints then read precomputed values with a fallback for schema rollout.

### Issues

**1. `isMissingProgressColumnError` duplicated across two files**

`functions/api/rating-history.ts` and `functions/api/stats.ts` both define identical `isMissingProgressColumnError` functions. This should live in a shared utility (e.g., alongside `shared/player-progress.ts`).

**2. Full history scan on every sync is expensive**

`recomputePlayerProgress` loads the *entire* `player_history` table for the season on every sync run. As data grows, this will become a bottleneck. Consider an incremental approach — the new snapshot only needs to update progress for players whose ratings changed in that snapshot, appending to existing counters.

**3. `loadFallbackProgressMetrics` also loads entire history**

The fallback in `stats.ts` (`loadFallbackProgressMetrics`) pulls every row from `player_history` joined with `player_latest` for the season into memory. For large seasons this could hit D1 row limits or cause OOM. This fallback is only needed during schema migration, but it's worth noting.

**4. SQL injection surface in `recomputePlayerProgress`**

The `sqlEscape` function is used for account IDs, but the pattern of building raw SQL with string interpolation (`CASE account_id WHEN '${escapedId}' THEN ...`) is fragile. If `sqlEscape` has any gaps, this is exploitable. Consider using parameterized queries or at minimum verify `sqlEscape` handles all edge cases.

**5. `current_win_streak` column is written but never read**

The schema adds `current_win_streak` and the sync computes it, but neither `stats.ts` nor `rating-history.ts` ever queries or returns it. If it's for future use, that's fine, but it's dead code for now.

**6. Fallback tiebreaker logic uses `-1` sentinel**

In `loadFallbackProgressMetrics`:
```ts
(progress.estimatedGames === (mostActive?.games ?? -1) && ...)
```
Using `-1` as the fallback when `mostActive` is null means on a tie with 0 games, `0 === -1` is false — which happens to work but is confusing. Using `0` or restructuring the condition would be clearer.

**7. Missing `ELSE` clause in batch `CASE` statements**

```sql
SET estimated_games = CASE account_id WHEN '...' THEN ... END
```
Without an `ELSE` clause, any `account_id` not in the batch but matched by the `WHERE IN` clause would be set to `NULL`. The `WHERE IN` filter should prevent this, but an explicit `ELSE estimated_games` would be safer.

### Minor / Style

- The try/catch pattern for schema migration (`ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN`) silently swallows all errors, not just "column already exists". Consider checking the error message.
- Comment numbering in `main()` was updated (steps 8→9, 9→10) — fine, but step 8's comment could be more specific about *when* this runs relative to the data it depends on.

### Positives

- Extracting `computePlayerProgressFromHistory` into `shared/player-progress.ts` is a clean separation
- The algorithm fix (counting only rating changes as games, not pure rank movement) is correct and well-motivated
- The fallback strategy for gradual schema rollout is pragmatic
- Good use of `ORDER BY ... position ASC` as tiebreaker for stats

### Verdict

The core logic is sound and the shared progress calculator is well-designed. The main concerns are the **full table scan on every sync** (scalability), the **duplicated helper**, and the **raw SQL interpolation pattern**. I'd recommend addressing at least #1 and #7 before merging, and planning for #2 as the dataset grows.

2. **`current_win_streak` 已移除** — schema 和代码中都去掉了这个未使用的字段
3. **CASE 语句加了 `ELSE`** — `prev_position_24h` 和 `prev_rating_24h` 的 CASE 加了 `ELSE prev_position_24h END` / `ELSE prev_rating_24h END`

```typescript
export function computePlayerProgressFromHistory<T extends RatingPointLike>(
  history: T[]
): PlayerProgress {
  let estimatedGames = 0;
  let currentWinStreak = 0;
  let longestWinStreak = 0;

  // For each rating point in history (starting from second)
  for (let i = 1; i < history.length; i++) {
    const delta = history[i].rating - history[i - 1].rating;

    if (delta > 0) {  // Rating increased = WIN
      estimatedGames++;
      currentWinStreak++;
      if (currentWinStreak > longestWinStreak) {

    }

}
```

问题很清楚了。D1 的 `/query` 端点不支持数组格式的 batch。`backfillPlayerProgress` 里两处 `queryD1(batch.map(...))` 传了数组，但 API 只接受单个 `{sql, params}` 对象。

看日志，sync 本身是成功的（player_latest 和 player_progress 都写入了 2841 行），只是 backfill 挂了。而 backfill 只在首次加列时触发，所以现在的状态是：
- 列已加好
- sync 增量数据已写入
- 但旧数据没有 backfill

修法是把 `backfillPlayerProgress` 里的参数化 batch 改成和其他地方一样的 inline values 拼接（用 `sqlEscape`），或者改成逐条调用。要我修吗？

### Evalite Silent Failure Mode

- Evalite (v0.19+) silently swallows errors thrown in `beforeAll` hooks. When `beforeAll` fails, all evals show `Score: -`, `Duration: 0ms`, and no error output.
- If evals show this pattern, the cause is almost always a thrown error during setup — typically a missing env var in `setupEvalRuntime` (which calls `requireEnv` for all model IDs).
- To diagnose: check that all required env vars are set, or temporarily wrap `beforeAll` contents in try/catch with `console.error` to surface the real error.

### project-md-files > Schema & Data Migration > SurrealDB Existing Data Migration (Explicit Exception Only)
### SurrealDB Existing Data Migration (Explicit Exception Only)

- Default project policy is still no backfills; only run existing-data migrations when explicitly requested by the user.
- Snapshot before mutation with `surreal export --ns <namespace> --db <database> <backup-file>`.
- Run data transforms in versioned `.surql` scripts applied via `bun migrate`.
- Use a transaction for multi-step migrations:
  - `BEGIN TRANSACTION;`
  - apply schema updates (`DEFINE ... OVERWRITE` / `ALTER`)
  - backfill with `UPDATE ... WHERE ...`
  - rewrite relationships with `RELATE` (do NOT use `CREATE` for `TYPE RELATION` tables)
  - clean old keys with `REMOVE FIELD ...; UPDATE ... UNSET ...;`
  - `COMMIT TRANSACTION;`
- In this codebase, represent missing values as omitted fields / `NONE` (never `null`) during data transforms.
- Validate scripts with `surreal validate <migration-file>` before apply if the `surreal` CLI is available.
- Verify result counts and shape after apply (`SELECT count() ...`, `INFO FOR TABLE ...`).

### project-md-files > Schema & Data Migration
## Schema & Data Migration

- This project does NOT maintain backwards compatibility with existing data. Schema changes are breaking.
- Do NOT write data migration or backfill scripts. Old data is discarded on schema changes.
- New fields should be required (not optional) from the start — no need for `option<...>` to accommodate pre-existing records.

### project-md-files > Schema & Data Migration > SurrealDB Schema Migration Workflow
### SurrealDB Schema Migration Workflow

- Create a versioned `.surql` migration script for each schema change.
- Migration filenames MUST use a zero-padded autoincrement numeric prefix, followed by an underscore and slug (for example `schema/migrations/0008_add_task_priority.surql`).
- Determine the next prefix by scanning `schema/migrations` and incrementing the highest existing prefix. Do NOT reuse or renumber existing migration files.
- Apply migrations with `bun migrate` — the migration runner (`schema/migrate.ts`) tracks applied migrations in a `_migration` table and only runs pending ones.
- Do NOT apply migrations manually via `surreal import` or raw HTTP calls — always use `bun migrate`.
- Wrap migration scripts in `BEGIN TRANSACTION; ... COMMIT TRANSACTION;` so they succeed or fail atomically.
- `DEFINE ANALYZER` cannot run inside a transaction in SurrealDB v3.0. Place it before the `BEGIN TRANSACTION;` block.
- Prefer `DEFINE ... OVERWRITE` or `ALTER TABLE` / `ALTER FIELD` for schema evolution; reserve `IF NOT EXISTS` for bootstrap-only creation.
- SurrealDB does NOT support `ALTER TABLE ... ADD FIELD`. To add fields to existing tables, use `DEFINE FIELD OVERWRITE <field> ON <table> TYPE <type>;`.
- When removing fields, update schema and stored rows in the same migration (`REMOVE FIELD ...; UPDATE ... UNSET ...;`).
- Verify applied schema with `INFO FOR TABLE <table>;` in the target namespace/database.

## project structure overview

### project-md-files > Server Architecture Overview > Chat Agent Architecture
### Chat Agent Architecture

The chat system uses a thin orchestrator pattern where a single top-level chat agent dispatches to specialized subagents. The knowledge graph is the communication bus — agents read from and write to the graph independently, never passing data directly between each other.

```
User Message
  │
  ├─→ Extraction Pipeline (always runs, Haiku)
  │     └─→ entities/relationships → SurrealDB graph
  │
  └─→ Chat Agent (Sonnet, thin orchestrator)
        ├─→ Direct tools (search, entity detail, decisions, observations)
        └─→ Subagent dispatch
              └─→ PM Agent (Haiku) → suggestions, observations → graph
```

**Two paths to the graph:**
| Source | Path | Why |
|--------|------|-----|
| User messages | Extraction pipeline (Haiku infers entities from unstructured text) | User input is unstructured |
| Agent output | Direct graph write (agents already have structured form) | Nothing to extract |

**Key files:**
- `chat/handler.ts` — `runChatAgent()`: streams chat agent responses with tool use
- `chat/context.ts` — `buildChatContext()` / `buildSystemPrompt()`: loads graph context, builds chat agent system prompt
- `chat/tools/index.ts` — `createChatAgentTools()`: registers all chat agent tools
- `chat/tools/types.ts` — `ChatToolExecutionContext`: actor-typed context (`chat_agent | mcp | pm_agent`)

### project-md-files > Server Architecture Overview > Product Manager Subagent
### Product Manager Subagent

The PM agent (`agents/pm/`) is the single authority on tasks, features, and project status. It uses the AI SDK's `ToolLoopAgent` class and composes shared tools from `chat/tools/`. It is invoked by the chat agent via `invoke_pm_agent` tool with an intent:

| Intent | When to use |
|--------|-------------|
| `plan_work` | User discusses goals, features, or work to be done |
| `check_status` | User asks about project status, progress, or blockers |
| `organize` | User wants to restructure or re-prioritize |
| `track_dependencies` | User asks about blocked items or dependency chains |

**Key files:**
- `agents/pm/agent.ts` — `runPmAgent()`: creates `ToolLoopAgent` with PM tools, returns structured JSON output
- `agents/pm/prompt.ts` — `buildPmSystemPrompt()`: loads workspace projects and observations
- `agents/pm/tools.ts` — `createPmTools()`: composes shared tools (search_entities, get_project_status, create_observation, suggest_work_items, create_work_item)

**PM output schema:** `{ summary, suggestions: WorkItemSuggestion[], updated, discarded, observations_created }`

The chat agent renders PM suggestions as `WorkItemSuggestionList` component blocks in the chat UI.

### project-md-files > Server Architecture Overview > Work Item Accept Flow
### Work Item Accept Flow

When the PM agent suggests work items, the chat agent renders them as `WorkItemSuggestionList` components. Users can accept or dismiss each item:

- Accept calls `POST /api/workspaces/:workspaceId/work-items/accept`
- The endpoint creates a `task` or `feature` record in SurrealDB with embedding and optional project linking
- Implemented in `entities/work-item-accept-route.ts`

## schema and migrations

### project-md-files > Schema & Data Migration > SurrealDB Schema Migration Workflow
### SurrealDB Schema Migration Workflow

- Create a versioned `.surql` migration script for each schema change.
- Migration filenames MUST use a zero-padded autoincrement numeric prefix, followed by an underscore and slug (for example `schema/migrations/0008_add_task_priority.surql`).
- Determine the next prefix by scanning `schema/migrations` and incrementing the highest existing prefix. Do NOT reuse or renumber existing migration files.
- Apply migrations with `bun migrate` — the migration runner (`schema/migrate.ts`) tracks applied migrations in a `_migration` table and only runs pending ones.
- Do NOT apply migrations manually via `surreal import` or raw HTTP calls — always use `bun migrate`.
- Wrap migration scripts in `BEGIN TRANSACTION; ... COMMIT TRANSACTION;` so they succeed or fail atomically.
- `DEFINE ANALYZER` cannot run inside a transaction in SurrealDB v3.0. Place it before the `BEGIN TRANSACTION;` block.
- Prefer `DEFINE ... OVERWRITE` or `ALTER TABLE` / `ALTER FIELD` for schema evolution; reserve `IF NOT EXISTS` for bootstrap-only creation.
- SurrealDB does NOT support `ALTER TABLE ... ADD FIELD`. To add fields to existing tables, use `DEFINE FIELD OVERWRITE <field> ON <table> TYPE <type>;`.
- When removing fields, update schema and stored rows in the same migration (`REMOVE FIELD ...; UPDATE ... UNSET ...;`).
- Verify applied schema with `INFO FOR TABLE <table>;` in the target namespace/database.

- Default project policy is still no backfills; only run existing-data migrations when explicitly requested by the user.

  - `BEGIN TRANSACTION;`
  - apply schema updates (`DEFINE ... OVERWRITE` / `ALTER`)
  - backfill with `UPDATE ... WHERE ...`
  - rewrite relationships with `RELATE` (do NOT use `CREATE` for `TYPE RELATION` tables)

- Validate scripts with `surreal validate <migration-file>` before apply if the `surreal` CLI is available.
- Verify result counts and shape after apply (`SELECT count() ...`, `INFO FOR TABLE ...`).

### project-md-files > Testing Setup > Evalite Silent Failure Mode
### Evalite Silent Failure Mode

- Evalite (v0.19+) silently swallows errors thrown in `beforeAll` hooks. When `beforeAll` fails, all evals show `Score: -`, `Duration: 0ms`, and no error output.
- If evals show this pattern, the cause is almost always a thrown error during setup — typically a missing env var in `setupEvalRuntime` (which calls `requireEnv` for all model IDs).
- To diagnose: check that all required env vars are set, or temporarily wrap `beforeAll` contents in try/catch with `console.error` to surface the real error.

1→# Brain
     2→
     3→**The operating system for autonomous organizations.**
     4→
     5→Your agents have amnesia. They can't talk to each other. You spend 80% of your time as a high-paid secretary, copy-pasting context between them. Brain is the self-correcting knowledge graph that gives your agents shared memory, governed autonomy, and verifiable intent.
     6→
     7→---
     8→
     9→## The Problem
    10→
    11→You are the integration layer between your AI agents.
    12→
    13→You already use AI agents. Your coding agent writes your code. Your chat assistant helps you think through architecture. Your editor agent autocompletes. But none of them share context.
    14→
    15→- Copy error logs from CI into your coding agent
    16→- Relay architecture decisions from a chat into your codebase
    17→- Manually track what was decided, what's blocked, what changed
    18→- Re-explain project state every time you start a new session
    19→- Context-switch between tools, losing continuity at every step
    20→
    21→Every agent you add makes it worse. Brain fixes this — not by replacing your agents, but by giving them shared memory.
    22→
    23→## Architecture
    24→
    25→Why a graph, not a message bus. Most platforms try "agent swarms" — agents messaging agents. That creates a game of telephone where instructions get distorted. The graph is the single source of truth.
    26→
    27→```text
    28→Human Layer
    29→  → Web Chat / Feed / Graph View / Terminal
    30→
    31→Agent Layer
    32→  → Architect / Strategist / Management / Coding (MCP) / Design Partner / Observer
    33→
    34→Graph Layer
    35→  → Projects / Decisions / Tasks / Observations / Features / Questions
    36→  → Suggestions / Conversations / Commits / Intents / Learnings
    37→  → Traces / Policies
    38→
    39→Auth Layer
    40→  → OAuth 2.1 / RAR (RFC 9396) / DPoP (RFC 9449) / Better Auth IdP
    41→
    42→Integration Layer
    43→  → GitHub / Slack / Git Hooks / MCP Protocol / ERC-8004
    44→```
    45→
    46→| Approach | Agent swarms / message buses | Knowledge graph (Brain) |
    47→|----------|------------------------------|------------------------|
    48→| Logic | Scripted workflows (if A, do B) | State-based graph (emergent logic) |
    49→| Memory | Ephemeral, session-based | Persistent, pruned, versioned |
    50→| Coordination | Agents message agents (telephone game) | Agents read/write to shared truth |
    51→| Verification | Assumes API calls work | Continuous telemetry (reality grounding) |
    52→| Autonomy | "Let it rip" (high risk of loops) | Authority scopes (risk-managed) |
    53→| Over time | Performance degrades | System gets smarter via learnings |
    54→| Security | Sandbox isolation (the "box") | Governance graph + sandbox (the "brain") |
    55→| Auditing | Log-based (text dumps) | Graph-based (hierarchical traces, machine-readable) |
    56→
    57→## Specialized Agents
    58→
    59→Each agent has a role, a domain, and authority scopes. They coordinate through the knowledge graph — not through you.
    60→
    61→- **Architect** — Technical decisions, system design, architecture constraints. Checks implementations against what was decided. Resolves conflicts between competing approaches.
    62→- **Strategist** — Market positioning, pricing, GTM, competitive response. Challenges product decisions against business viability.
    63→- **Management** — Task tracking, priority management, execution velocity. Flags blocked work, stale decisions, and resource conflicts.
    64→- **Coding Agents (via MCP)** — Your existing tools (Cursor, Aider, Codex, Claude Code) connected to the graph. Context injected on session start. Decisions, observations, and questions flow back automatically.
    65→- **Design Partner** — Brainstorms product ideas, asks probing questions, identifies gaps. Shapes vague ideas into structured projects, features, and decisions.
    66→- **Observer** — Scans the graph for patterns nobody asked about. Stale decisions, cross-project conflicts, missing coverage, priority drift.
    67→
    68→## How Coordination Works
    69→
    70→No agent messages another agent. They write structured signals to the knowledge graph. The graph makes it visible to the right agent at the right time.
    71→
    72→1. **Coding agent notices a contradiction.** While implementing rate limiting, a coding agent detects that `src/billing/api.ts` uses REST — but the graph has a confirmed decision to standardize on tRPC. It logs an observation.
    73→2. **Architect agent sees it on next context load.** The Architect checks the observation against constraints. Confirms the contradiction is real. Generates a suggestion: "Migrate billing API to tRPC, or revisit the standardization decision."
    74→3. **Suggestion surfaces in your feed.** You see the suggestion with full provenance — the observation, the contradicted decision, the Architect's reasoning. You accept it. A migration task is created with one click.
    75→4. **Next coding session picks up the task.** The migration task appears in the coding agent's context. It decomposes into subtasks, works through them, and status rolls up automatically. No human copied anything between tabs.
    76→
    77→## Key Concepts
    78→
    79→- **Decisions** — Every decision is tracked — who made it, why, and what alternatives were considered. Agents propose. Humans confirm.
    80→- **Observations** — Agents surface contradictions, gaps, patterns, and risks as they work. Observations accumulate and compound into actionable suggestions.
    81→- **Suggestions** — Agents tell you what you should be thinking about. Accept a suggestion and it becomes a task, decision, or feature — with full trace back to the evidence.
    82→- **Projects, Features & Tasks** — Work breaks down hierarchically. Agents decompose tasks at runtime. Status rolls up automatically.
    83→- **Questions** — When an agent doesn't know, it asks instead of guessing. You answer. The answer becomes a decision in the graph.
    84→- **Conversations** — Every chat produces structured knowledge. Conversations group by project automatically.
    85→- **Commits** — Code is linked to the decisions and tasks it implements. Contradictions are caught before they land.
    86→- **Intents** — Every agent action starts as an intent — a structured request in the graph. Intents carry the full authorization context and are evaluated against authority scopes before execution.
    87→- **Authority Scopes** — Control what each agent can do without asking. Start restrictive. Expand trust over time.
    88→- **Learnings** — Behavioral rules injected into agent prompts at runtime. The system gets smarter as it works, not dumber.
    89→- **Identity** — One person across all tools. Your Slack, GitHub, and terminal sessions all resolve to the same identity.
    90→- **Agent Sessions** — Every session is remembered. The next agent knows what the last one did.
    91→- **Traces** — Every agent execution is a graph-native call tree. Subagent spawns, tool calls, and decisions form a hierarchical trace you can traverse, query, and audit. Forensic debugging is a graph query, not grep.
    92→- **Policies** — Deterministic governance rules stored as graph nodes, not prompt text. Each policy carries typed rules, scopes, and approval requirements. The Authorizer evaluates intents against the policy graph before minting tokens — no prompt rewriting needed.
    93→
    94→## Reliability: Solving the Three Drifts
    95→
    96→Autonomous systems don't fail from lack of intelligence. They fail from drift — slow divergence between what the system believes and what's actually true.
    97→
    98→- **Context Drift** — Decisions made in v1.0 become poison for v2.0. Brain uses temporal decay — nodes that aren't referenced lose weight over time. The Observer agent runs conflict resolution loops, flagging stale decisions that contradict recent commits.
    99→- **Authority Drift** — Too autonomous = dangerous. Too locked down = a dashboard. Brain uses tiered authority scopes — from zero-human atomic actions to multi-model consensus for high-stakes moves. Agents operate within risk budgets, not permission checkboxes.
   100→- **Reality Drift** — If the Brain only reads its own graph, it's a delusion engine. Observer agents perform truth audits — checking claims against actual state via webhooks and integrations. When reality diverges from the graph, the system triggers a desync alert.
   101→
   102→## Verifiable Autonomy
   103→
   104→Most autonomous platforms are black boxes. Brain is a signed logic trace. Every decision, every dollar, every line of code has a provenance chain back to the intent that authorized it.
   105→
   106→- **Governance telemetry** — Every decision is a node with a UUID, author, timestamp, and reasoning. Auditors can query the graph directly.
   107→- **Signed intent chains** — When an agent spends money or merges code, the graph records which intent authorized it, which authority scope permitted it, and which human approved it.
   108→- **Hierarchical traces** — Agent executions are graph-native call trees. A subagent spawn becomes a root trace; each tool call, message, and decision is a child node. Traverse the full execution path with a graph query — from intent to final action.
   109→- **Policy-as-graph** — Governance rules are structured nodes with typed rules, scopes, and approval requirements. The Authorizer evaluates intents against the policy graph before minting tokens — deterministic, auditable, and updateable without touching a single prompt.
   110→- **The "Judge" pattern** — High-stakes actions go through an Authorizer Agent that validates intents against policy constraints before minting scoped tokens. The worker never sees master keys.
   111→
   112→## Open Source
   113→
   114→The knowledge graph that coordinates your agents shouldn't be a black box you rent. It should be infrastructure you own, inspect, and extend.
   115→
   116→- **Full source access** — Graph engine, MCP server, agent prompts, extraction pipeline. Every line.
   117→- **No vendor lock-in** — Your data lives in your SurrealDB instance. Export anytime. Migrate anytime.
   118→- **Extend everything** — Custom agent types, observation categories, feed cards, MCP tools.
   119→- **Community-driven** — Agent prompts, authority scope templates, and integrations contributed by users.
   120→
   121→## Tech Stack
   122→
   123→| Layer | Technology |
   124→|-------|-----------|
   125→| Graph | SurrealDB |
   126→| Backend | Bun (`Bun.serve`) · TypeScript |

     5→## Data Value Contract
     6→
     7→- Never persist, publish, or return `null` for domain data values (Surreal records, API payloads, events, UI state).
     8→- Absence must be represented by omitted optional fields only (`field?: Type`), not by `null`.
     9→- If `null` appears in domain data, treat it as a contract violation and fix the producer. Do NOT sanitize/coerce it at consumers.

    11→## TypeScript Conventions
    12→
    13→- Do NOT use `null`. Use `undefined` via optional properties (`field?: Type`) instead.
    14→- Do NOT create wrapper/helper functions for simple operations. Cast directly with `as`.
    15→- Type result payloads once and avoid repetitive per-field casting.
    16→- Do NOT use module-level mutable singletons (e.g. `let cache` at file scope) for caching or shared state. Module-level state is shared across the entire process — when multiple server instances run concurrently (e.g. smoke tests with `--concurrent`), they silently corrupt each other. Pass shared state via dependency injection or use per-instance caches scoped to the owning object.

    20→## LLM Tool Definitions (Vercel AI SDK)
    21→
    22→- Tool `description` is for *what the tool does* and *when to use it*. Keep it concise.
    23→- Parameter-level guidance belongs on `.describe()` in the Zod `inputSchema`, not in the tool description or system prompt.
    24→- For enums, put per-value guidance in `.describe()` on the enum field — the `ai` SDK converts Zod `.describe()` to JSON Schema `description` at every level.
    25→- Do NOT duplicate tool descriptions or parameter guidance in the system prompt. The LLM already receives tool definitions via the `tools` API parameter.
    26→- System prompt should only contain information the LLM cannot get from tool definitions: dynamic context, rendering format instructions, and cross-cutting architectural rules.

    28→## Extraction Schema (Structured Output)
    29→
    30→- Azure/OpenRouter structured output requires every property in `properties` to be listed in `required`. Zod `.optional()` fields are excluded from `required` in the generated JSON schema, causing provider rejection.
    31→- Do NOT use `.optional()` in `extractionResultSchema` or its nested entity schemas (`app/src/server/extraction/schema.ts`).
    32→- To represent absence, add a `"none"` sentinel to the enum and strip it to `undefined` via `.transform()` after parsing. The transform is applied during Zod validation but does not affect the JSON schema sent to the provider.
    33→- Existing pattern: `assignee_name` and `resolvedFromMessageId` use union variants (each variant has the field as required) instead of optional fields.

    35→## Schema & Data Migration
    36→
    37→- This project does NOT maintain backwards compatibility with existing data. Schema changes are breaking.
    38→- Do NOT write data migration or backfill scripts. Old data is discarded on schema changes.
    39→- New fields should be required (not optional) from the start — no need for `option<...>` to accommodate pre-existing records.
    40→
    41→### SurrealDB Schema Migration Workflow
    42→
    43→- Create a versioned `.surql` migration script for each schema change.
    44→- Migration filenames MUST use a zero-padded autoincrement numeric prefix, followed by an underscore and slug (for example `schema/migrations/0008_add_task_priority.surql`).
    45→- Determine the next prefix by scanning `schema/migrations` and incrementing the highest existing prefix. Do NOT reuse or renumber existing migration files.
    46→- Apply migrations with `bun migrate` — the migration runner (`schema/migrate.ts`) tracks applied migrations in a `_migration` table and only runs pending ones.
    47→- Do NOT apply migrations manually via `surreal import` or raw HTTP calls — always use `bun migrate`.
    48→- Wrap migration scripts in `BEGIN TRANSACTION; ... COMMIT TRANSACTION;` so they succeed or fail atomically.
    49→- `DEFINE ANALYZER` cannot run inside a transaction in SurrealDB v3.0. Place it before the `BEGIN TRANSACTION;` block.
    50→- Prefer `DEFINE ... OVERWRITE` or `ALTER TABLE` / `ALTER FIELD` for schema evolution; reserve `IF NOT EXISTS` for bootstrap-only creation.
    51→- SurrealDB does NOT support `ALTER TABLE ... ADD FIELD`. To add fields to existing tables, use `DEFINE FIELD OVERWRITE <field> ON <table> TYPE <type>;`.
    52→- When removing fields, update schema and stored rows in the same migration (`REMOVE FIELD ...; UPDATE ... UNSET ...;`).
    53→- Verify applied schema with `INFO FOR TABLE <table>;` in the target namespace/database.
    54→
    55→### SurrealDB Existing Data Migration (Explicit Exception Only)
    56→
    57→- Default project policy is still no backfills; only run existing-data migrations when explicitly requested by the user.
    58→- Snapshot before mutation with `surreal export --ns <namespace> --db <database> <backup-file>`.
    59→- Run data transforms in versioned `.surql` scripts applied via `bun migrate`.
    60→- Use a transaction for multi-step migrations:
    61→  - `BEGIN TRANSACTION;`
    62→  - apply schema updates (`DEFINE ... OVERWRITE` / `ALTER`)
    63→  - backfill with `UPDATE ... WHERE ...`
    64→  - rewrite relationships with `RELATE` (do NOT use `CREATE` for `TYPE RELATION` tables)
    65→  - clean old keys with `REMOVE FIELD ...; UPDATE ... UNSET ...;`
    66→  - `COMMIT TRANSACTION;`
    67→- In this codebase, represent missing values as omitted fields / `NONE` (never `null`) during data transforms.
    68→- Validate scripts with `surreal validate <migration-file>` before apply if the `surreal` CLI is available.
    69→- Verify result counts and shape after apply (`SELECT count() ...`, `INFO FOR TABLE ...`).
    70→
    71→## Fire-and-Forget & Inflight Tracking
    72→
    73→- Do NOT use `void` for fire-and-forget DB operations in route handlers. Background work that uses the SurrealDB connection will fail with `ConnectionUnavailableError` when smoke tests close the DB in `afterAll`.
    74→- Route-level async work (e.g. `processGitCommits`, `processChatMessage`) must be tracked via `deps.inflight.track(promise)`. The `InflightTracker` (`runtime/types.ts`) lets smoke tests `drain()` pending work before closing connections.
    75→- Nested async work inside tracked parents (e.g. `seedDescriptionEntry`, `fireDescriptionUpdates`, `persistEmbeddings`) should use `await ... .catch(() => undefined)` instead of `void`. Since the parent is already background work, awaiting doesn't affect user-facing latency.
    76→- When adding new background DB operations in route handlers, always use `deps.inflight.track()` or `await` within an already-tracked parent.
    77→
    78→## SurrealDB EVENT Webhook Timing
    79→
    80→- SurrealDB `DEFINE EVENT` HTTP webhooks can fire before the triggering write is visible to other requests.
    81→- Prefer `DEFINE EVENT ... ASYNC` for webhook-style side effects so callback execution runs after the triggering write commits.
    82→- Use `RETRY <n>` on webhook events to reduce transient callback/network flakiness.
    83→- For intent authorization (`draft -> pending_auth`), avoid synchronous webhook flows that immediately re-read/update the same intent unless the event is `ASYNC`.
    84→- If a webhook path must do DB follow-up without `ASYNC`, wait briefly for the triggering transition to commit before applying routing/state transitions.
    85→- If async follow-up work is needed in route handlers, track it with `deps.inflight.track(...)`.
    86→
    87→## Failure Handling
    88→
    89→- Do NOT add fallback logic that masks invalid state, malformed payloads, or contract violations.
    90→- Fail fast: throw immediately when required data is missing or does not match the expected shape.
    91→- Prefer explicit hard failures over silent degradation, synthetic defaults, or "best effort" recovery.
    92→- Only introduce fallback behavior when explicitly requested, and document the reason in code comments.
    93→- Never silently ignore errors (e.g. empty `.catch(() => {})`). Always surface them via logging or re-throw.
    94→
    95→## Schema Awareness
    96→
    97→- Always read `schema/surreal-schema.surql` before writing queries, seed data, or any code that creates/updates SurrealDB records. The schema defines required fields, types, and relations — guessing leads to silent `SCHEMAFULL` rejections.

    99→## DPoP Acceptance Test Infrastructure
   100→
   101→- All MCP endpoints require DPoP (Demonstration of Proof-of-Possession) authentication. Use `createTestUserWithMcp()` from `acceptance-test-kit.ts` — it generates a key pair, creates identity + workspace + intent records, acquires a DPoP-bound token, and returns `mcpFetch` for authenticated requests.
   102→- **Workspace binding**: The DPoP token contains a `urn:brain:workspace` claim. The middleware (`dpop-middleware.ts:311`) extracts the workspace from the JWT claim, NOT the URL path parameter. All MCP endpoint authorization is scoped to this claim.
   103→- **`member_of` edge required**: The DPoP middleware calls `lookupWorkspace()` which queries `SELECT in FROM member_of WHERE out = $ws LIMIT 1`. Without a `member_of` relation edge between identity and workspace, all MCP requests return 401 "Workspace not found". `createTestUserWithMcp()` creates this edge automatically.
   104→- **Workspace mismatch pitfall**: If a test creates a workspace via the API (`POST /api/workspaces`) and then acquires a DPoP token via `createTestUserWithMcp()`, the token is bound to a *different* workspace. MCP endpoints will return 404 for resources in the API-created workspace. Fix: pass `{ workspaceId }` to `createTestUserWithMcp()` to bind the token to the pre-existing workspace, or use `user.workspaceId` for all resource creation.
   105→- **Pattern**: Create test user first (`createTestUserWithMcp`), then create tasks/projects in `user.workspaceId`. Do NOT create a separate workspace via API unless you pass its ID to `createTestUserWithMcp`.
   106→- **`mcpFetch` vs `mcpHeaders`**: Always use `user.mcpFetch(path, { body })` — it creates a fresh DPoP proof per request. The `mcpHeaders` property is deprecated and will fail because DPoP proofs are single-use.
   107→

   171→### Chat Agent Architecture
   172→
   173→The chat system uses a thin orchestrator pattern where a single top-level chat agent dispatches to specialized subagents. The knowledge graph is the communication bus — agents read from and write to the graph independently, never passing data directly between each other.
   174→
   175→```
   176→User Message
   177→  │
   178→  ├─→ Extraction Pipeline (always runs, Haiku)
   179→  │     └─→ entities/relationships → SurrealDB graph
   180→  │
   181→  └─→ Chat Agent (Sonnet, thin orchestrator)
   182→        ├─→ Direct tools (search, entity detail, decisions, observations)
   183→        └─→ Subagent dispatch
   184→              └─→ PM Agent (Haiku) → suggestions, observations → graph
   185→```
   186→
   187→**Two paths to the graph:**
   188→| Source | Path | Why |
   189→|--------|------|-----|
   190→| User messages | Extraction pipeline (Haiku infers entities from unstructured text) | User input is unstructured |
   191→| Agent output | Direct graph write (agents already have structured form) | Nothing to extract |
   192→
   193→**Key files:**
   194→- `chat/handler.ts` — `runChatAgent()`: streams chat agent responses with tool use
   195→- `chat/context.ts` — `buildChatContext()` / `buildSystemPrompt()`: loads graph context, builds chat agent system prompt
   196→- `chat/tools/index.ts` — `createChatAgentTools()`: registers all chat agent tools
   197→- `chat/tools/types.ts` — `ChatToolExecutionContext`: actor-typed context (`chat_agent | mcp | pm_agent`)
   198→
   199→### Chat Agent Tools
   200→
   201→| Tool | Purpose |
   202→|------|---------|
   203→| `search_entities` | Search workspace entities by text query |
   204→| `get_entity_detail` | Fetch entity with relationships and provenance |
   205→| `get_project_status` | Project task/decision/question aggregation |
   206→| `get_conversation_history` | Load recent conversation messages |
   207→| `create_provisional_decision` | Draft a decision for user review |
   208→| `confirm_decision` | Finalize a decision (requires explicit user auth) |
   209→| `resolve_decision` | Mark a decision as resolved |
   210→| `check_constraints` | Validate decision constraints |
   211→| `create_observation` | Create observation for risks/conflicts/signals |
   212→| `acknowledge_observation` | Mark observation as reviewed |
   213→| `resolve_observation` | Close a resolved observation |
   214→| `invoke_pm_agent` | Delegate to PM subagent |
   215→
   216→### Shared Tool Layer
   217→
   218→Tools live in `chat/tools/` as composable building blocks. Any agent (chat agent, PM subagent, future subagents) can compose the tools it needs. Key shared tools for work item management:

   220→| Tool | File | Purpose |
